name: Scorecard
what: An internal research tool for the njct portfolio. It shows where any website's visitors come from, from search and ads to links and social mentions, so each product's marketing starts from what already works.
glance: Traffic, ads, organic search, links, mentions and apps for each site
Up to ten sites side by side, sorted by rank, growth, visits or ad spend
How each site gets its traffic, with a confidence level and the evidence
archHi:
Scorecard is a research dashboard that works out how a website gets its traffic. Every site goes through the same analysis, in the same order:

  1. Profile. Category, pricing model, launch date with the evidence for it, the company, its technology and its apps.
  2. Size and trend. Daily traffic rank, monthly visits, countries, and how visitors behave once they arrive.
  3. Traffic mix. The share of visits from direct, search, paid, social, referrals and email. The mix decides where the rest of the analysis looks hardest.
  4. Paid. Ads found in the public ad libraries, the keywords and brands it bids on, and an estimate of monthly ad spend.
  5. Search and links. The keywords it ranks for, the searches similar sites win that it does not, and the domains linking to it over time.
  6. Mentions. Posts, videos, listings and reviews that name the site, channel by channel.
  7. Read-out. A few lines on how the site gets its traffic, with a confidence level and the evidence behind each.

Sites sit in one sortable table and open side by side, up to ten at a time. Every figure names its source and date, so any finding can be checked, and the next site is analysed the same way. The findings feed the marketing of the other products in this portfolio.
arch:
A Python collector gathers the data and writes the dashboard's JSON data files, and the dashboard draws them with D3. Sources are chosen free first: a paid or credit source is used only where every free route failed, or where it adds depth a free route cannot give.

DataSource
Traffic rankTranco top-sites list, daily; Chrome UX Report top 1M, monthly
Visits, channel mix, countries, audienceSimilarweb public estimates, collected through Apify
Phone and desktop splitChrome UX Report, weekly
Organic search, keyword gap, top pages, linksDataForSEO Labs and Backlinks
AdsGoogle Ads Transparency Center and the Meta, Microsoft, LinkedIn and TikTok ad libraries
MentionsTikTok, Instagram, Reddit, X, YouTube, Hacker News, Product Hunt and directory listings
ProfileThe site's own pages, Wayback captures, certificate records, App Store, Google Play and Trustpilot
  • One part per source. The collector runs a fixed sequence of parts for each domain, and each part owns its own dashboard files. Parts that combine evidence run after the parts they read.
  • Raw responses are kept. Every part saves its raw responses per site and reads them back on the next run, so a re-run costs nothing. A refresh flag re-collects.
  • Paid calls are capped per run. Every paid call passes a guard that stops the run before a service would go past its cap, and each call's cost goes into a spend ledger. A dry run lists every paid call a run would make, with its estimated cost, and makes none.
  • Mentions are graded. Brand names collide, so a hit counts only when it names the domain, the site's own handle or one of its artefacts, such as an export filename that creators leave in their captions. Hits on the brand word alone are listed for review, and known collisions are excluded. Counts show confirmed hits only.
  • A verdict per ad platform. Eleven platforms each get Yes, No or Unknown from the platform's ad library, tracking code found on the site and campaign tags in archived links, with the reason and a confidence level. A platform whose library covers only the EU, or that has no library, stays Unknown unless the site's ads turn up there.
  • Ads are sampled at both ends. For each format the gallery keeps the newest ads and the longest-running ones, and long runners are marked. Text ads that the library stores as images are read with macOS Vision.
  • Ad spend is an estimate with its working. Visits × paid share × the cost per click of the site's top keywords, plus display, shown as a low-to-high range with the calculation beside it.
  • Every row carries its date. Rows are stamped with the date they were collected, and every panel names its source. A channel searched with nothing found shows 0, and one not yet checked shows a dash. Known limits print beside the figure: Similarweb's two-month lag, Tranco's 30-day average, and a device split that counts Chrome only.
  • Merges are per site. A merge replaces one site's rows and keeps every other site's, after copying the dashboard's data folder to a backup.
  • Re-runs are requests. Each analysis runs once. Update now and monthly auto-update are recorded in the dashboard's database, and queued requests run on the next collection pass. Sites that appear as a similar site or a targeted brand for two or more tracked sites are listed as suggestions.
proc:
• A Python collector and a D3 dashboard. The collector is a run script with one module per family of sources. It loads pages in Playwright's headless Chromium, reads ad images through a small Swift helper that calls macOS Vision, and sends pages that block automated reads, such as the ad libraries, through a real-browser reader on an always-on Mac mini. DataForSEO supplies the search, keyword-gap and link data, paid per call from a deposit. The dashboard is one page drawn with D3 from the JSON data files, kept as a private artifact whose database holds update requests and settings.
  • Pipes and filters. Each part reads raw responses and the outputs of the parts before it, and writes its own files. The ad-platform verdict is a filter over the ad-library, site-scan, archive and Similarweb outputs.
  • Idempotent, cached collection. Raw responses are a read-through cache per site, and writing a part's rows replaces that site's rows and keeps every other site's. Running the same collection twice changes nothing and costs nothing.
  • Dry-run planning with spend caps. Each paid call is declared to a guard before it is made. In a dry run the guard records the plan and skips the call; in a real run it enforces a per-service cap and writes the cost to the ledger.
  • Data provenance on every value. Each row carries its collection date and each panel its source and method, and the dashboard's sources section lists where every number comes from.
  • Precision-first entity matching. Mentions and ads are matched on the domain, the handle and known artefacts. Each site's profile records its brand word and its collision patterns, so a common word never inflates a count.
  • Secrets read once into memory. All keys are read in one vault call per run and held only in that process's memory. A dry run reads none.
